usage: The most common greeting in Estonia. It works almost everywhere: with friends, colleagues, neighbours, shop assistants — both informal and formal.
examples: Tere, Mari! — Hi, Mari! • Tere! Kuidas läheb? — Hello! How are you?
reply: Tere! — Hi! / Hello!

usage: Another greeting for any time of day, literally “(wishing you) health”. Older people use it a lot. Don’t mix it up with Terviseks! — that is what you say when raising a glass or when someone sneezes.
examples: Tervist, naaber! — Hello, neighbour! • Tervist! Kaua pole näinud! — Hi! Long time no see!
reply: Tervist! — Hello!

usage: An informal word for friends, family and people your age. It works both when you meet and when you leave. In messages people often just write tsau.
examples: Tšau, Mari! Mis teed? — Hi, Mari! What are you up to? • Ma hakkan minema. Tšau! — I have to go. Bye!
reply: Tšau! — Hi! / Bye!

usage: An informal greeting, just like English “hey”. Usually used with people you know and in messages.
examples: Hei, kuidas läheb? — Hey, how are you? • Hei, kas sul on hetk aega? — Hey, have you got a minute?
reply: Hei! — Hey!

usage: An affectionate, playful “hiya” formed from tere. Used with family, close friends and children.
examples: Terekest, kallis! — Hiya, darling! • Terekest kõigile! — Hi, everyone!
reply: Terekest! — Hiya!

usage: The usual question after a greeting. Estonians tend to answer briefly, without going into detail. Formal or plural: Kuidas teil läheb?
examples: Tere! Kuidas läheb? — Hi! How are you? • Kuidas teil läheb? — How are you? (formal)
reply: Hästi, aitäh! Ja sul? — Fine, thanks! And you? • Normaalselt. — Not bad.

usage: A friendly question when you meet someone — especially if you haven’t seen each other for a while.
examples: Tere, Jaan! Mis uudist? — Hi, Jaan! What’s new?
reply: Ei midagi erilist. — Nothing special. • Kõik vanaviisi. — Same as always.

usage: When you meet someone you know, especially after a long time. Formal or plural: Rõõm teid näha!
examples: Tere, Kati! Rõõm sind näha! — Hi, Kati! Nice to see you! • Rõõm teid näha! — Nice to see you! (formal)
reply: Mul on ka hea meel! — I’m glad too!

usage: Used to greet guests, new colleagues and tourists. You will often see it on signs and websites.
examples: Tere tulemast Eestisse! — Welcome to Estonia! • Tere tulemast meile! — Welcome to our place!
reply: Aitäh! — Thank you!

usage: A warm wish when saying goodbye or at the end of a letter — to a friend or a colleague. Other goodbyes: Head aega! — “Goodbye!”, Nägemist! — “See you!”.
examples: Aitäh ja kõike head! — Thank you and all the best! • Kõike head sünnipäevaks! — All the best on your birthday!
reply: Aitäh, sulle ka! — Thanks, you too!

usage: A wish for someone who is studying. Short form: Edu! (“Good luck!”). Before an exam people say Edu eksamil!
examples: Edu õppimisel! — Good luck with your studies! • Homme on eksam? Edu! — Exam tomorrow? Good luck!
reply: Aitäh! — Thank you!

usage: A traditional Estonian wish for someone who is working: a neighbour in the garden, a craftsman, a colleague. Short form: Jõudu! There is a special phrase to answer it.
examples: Tere, naaber! Jõudu tööle! — Hello, neighbour! Strength for your work! • Jõudu! — Keep it up!
reply: Jõudu tarvis! — Strength is needed! (the customary answer)

usage: A morning greeting — until about 11 o’clock. Polite and suitable for everyone.
examples: Tere hommikust, õpetaja! — Good morning, teacher! • Tere hommikust! Kas soovite kohvi? — Good morning! Would you like some coffee?
reply: Tere hommikust! — Good morning!

usage: A short, casual “good morning” for people close to you: family, friends, colleagues.
examples: Hommikust! Kas magasid hästi? — Morning! Did you sleep well? • Hommikust kõigile! — Morning, everyone!
reply: Hommikust! — Morning!

usage: A polite daytime greeting — roughly from 11 to 18. It sounds a little more formal than Tere.
examples: Tere päevast! Kuidas saan teid aidata? — Good afternoon! How can I help you? • Tere päevast, härra Tamm! — Good afternoon, Mr Tamm!
reply: Tere päevast! — Good afternoon!

usage: An evening greeting — from about 18 o’clock. Late at night you can simply say Tere.
examples: Tere õhtust! Laud kahele, palun. — Good evening! A table for two, please. • Tere õhtust, head vaatajad! — Good evening, dear viewers!
reply: Tere õhtust! — Good evening!

usage: Said when leaving late in the evening or before going to bed. It is not a greeting: if you meet someone at night, say Tere or Tere õhtust.
examples: Head ööd ja head und! — Good night and sleep well! • Aitäh, head ööd! — Thanks, good night!
reply: Head ööd! — Good night!

usage: A goodbye wish during the day: in a shop, after a conversation, at the end of a phone call.
examples: Aitäh, head päeva! — Thank you, have a nice day! • Head päeva ka teile! — Have a nice day too!
reply: Aitäh, samuti! — Thanks, same to you!

usage: A warm goodbye wish during the day — a little more heartfelt than Head päeva.
examples: Ilusat päeva sulle! — Have a lovely day! • Aitäh! Ilusat päeva! — Thank you! Have a lovely day!
reply: Aitäh, sulle ka! — Thanks, you too!

usage: A goodbye wish in the evening — for example when leaving work or a shop.
examples: Aitäh, head õhtut! — Thanks, have a nice evening! • Head õhtut ja kohtumiseni! — Have a nice evening and see you soon!
reply: Aitäh, samuti! — Thanks, same to you!

usage: Said before a meal or to someone who is eating. In Estonia lunch is usually around midday.
examples: Supp on laual. Head isu! — The soup is on the table. Enjoy your meal! • Head isu kõigile! — Enjoy your meal, everyone!
reply: Aitäh, sulle ka! — Thanks, you too!

english: Have a good start to the week!
usage: A Monday wish for colleagues and friends, often in messages.
examples: Tere hommikust ja head nädala algust! — Good morning and have a good start to the week! • Head nädala algust kõigile! — Have a good start to the week, everyone!
reply: Aitäh, samuti! — Thanks, same to you!

usage: A Friday or Saturday wish for colleagues, friends or a shop assistant.
examples: Head nädalavahetust! Näeme esmaspäeval. — Have a nice weekend! See you on Monday. • Aitäh ja head nädalavahetust! — Thanks and have a nice weekend!
reply: Aitäh, sulle ka! — Thanks, you too!

usage: A Sunday wish. Mõnus means “pleasant, cosy” — a calm, unhurried day.
examples: Mõnusat pühapäeva sulle! — Have a cosy Sunday! • Mõnusat pühapäeva ja puhka hästi! — Have a cosy Sunday and get some rest!
reply: Aitäh, samuti! — Thanks, you too!

usage: A spring wish (March to May), common in letters and cards.
examples: Ilusat kevadet ja palju päikest! — Have a lovely spring with lots of sunshine! • Soovin teile ilusat kevadet! — I wish you a lovely spring!
reply: Aitäh, samuti! — Thanks, same to you!

usage: A summer wish (June to August). Especially common at the end of the school year and before holidays.
examples: Ilusat suve! Näeme sügisel. — Have a lovely summer! See you in autumn. • Ilusat suve ja head puhkust! — Have a lovely summer and a good holiday!
reply: Aitäh, sulle ka! — Thanks, you too!

usage: An autumn wish (September to November), common in letters and cards.
examples: Ilusat sügist ja palju energiat! — Have a lovely autumn and lots of energy! • Soovin teile ilusat sügist! — I wish you a lovely autumn!
reply: Aitäh, samuti! — Thanks, same to you!

usage: 14 February in Estonia is sõbrapäev, “friends’ day”. Cards and small gifts go not only to loved ones but also to friends, classmates and colleagues.
examples: Head sõbrapäeva, sõber! — Happy Friendship Day, friend! • Head sõbrapäeva kõigile! — Happy Friendship Day, everyone!
reply: Aitäh, sulle ka! — Thanks, you too!

usage: 24 February is Estonia’s main national holiday: the Republic of Estonia was proclaimed on this day in 1918. The flag is raised in the morning, and in the evening people watch the President’s reception on TV.
examples: Head vabariigi aastapäeva! — Happy Independence Day! • Palju õnne, Eesti! — Happy birthday, Estonia!
reply: Aitäh, samuti! — Thanks, same to you!

usage: 14 March is Estonian Language Day, the birthday of the poet Kristjan Jaak Peterson. A great excuse to say a few phrases in Estonian!
examples: Head emakeelepäeva! — Happy Mother Tongue Day! • Täna räägime ainult eesti keeles! — Today we speak only Estonian!
reply: Aitäh! — Thank you!

usage: 23–24 June is the biggest summer celebration: bonfires (jaanituli), songs and the shortest night of the year. Casually: Ilusat jaani!
examples: Head jaanipäeva! Kas lähed jaanitulele? — Happy Midsummer! Are you going to the bonfire? • Ilusat jaani! — Have a lovely Midsummer!
reply: Aitäh, samuti! — Thanks, you too!

usage: 1 September is the start of the school year. Children go to school with flowers, and adults wish them success.
examples: Head teadmistepäeva ja edukat kooliaastat! — Happy Knowledge Day and a successful school year! • Head teadmistepäeva! — Happy Knowledge Day!
reply: Aitäh! — Thank you!

usage: Christmas (jõulud) is the main winter holiday. The most important evening is 24 December, jõululaupäev. People exchange wishes from about 20 to 26 December.
examples: Häid jõule ja head uut aastat! — Merry Christmas and a happy New Year! • Rahulikke jõule! — Have a peaceful Christmas!
reply: Aitäh, samuti! — Thanks, same to you!

usage: A general wish for the festive season — from Christmas to New Year.
examples: Häid pühi teile kõigile! — Happy holidays to you all! • Aitäh ja häid pühi! — Thanks and happy holidays!
reply: Aitäh, samuti! — Thanks, same to you!

usage: Said on the last day of the year and in the first days of January.
examples: Head uut aastat! — Happy New Year! • Head uut aastat ja palju õnne! — Happy New Year and all the best!
reply: Aitäh, samuti! — Thanks, same to you!

usage: A short goodbye wish during the day — common in shops and cafés. Same as Head päeva.
examples: Aitäh, kena päeva! — Thanks, have a nice day! • Kena päeva teilegi! — Have a nice day too!
reply: Aitäh, teile ka! — Thanks, you too!

usage: A warm goodbye wish in the evening — the partner of Ilusat päeva. Similar to Head õhtut.
examples: Aitäh, ilusat õhtut! — Thanks, have a lovely evening! • Ilusat õhtut sulle! — Have a lovely evening!
reply: Aitäh, sulle ka! — Thanks, you too!

usage: A warm wish for someone you know well: “take care”, “you’ve got this”. Often used as a goodbye. Tubli means “well done” — you can praise someone with just one word: Tubli!
examples: Ole tubli ja hoia ennast! — Take care of yourself! • Head aega, ole tubli! — Bye, take care!
reply: Aitäh, sina ka! — Thanks, you too!

english: Have a good end of the year!
usage: Said in the last days of December — until midnight on the 31st. After midnight people say Head uut aastat!
examples: Head vana aasta lõppu ja head uut aastat! — Have a good end of the year and a happy New Year! • Aitäh, head vana aasta lõppu teilegi! — Thanks, a good end of the year to you too!
reply: Aitäh, samuti! — Thanks, same to you!

english: Have a good start to the school year!
usage: A wish for pupils, students and teachers in the first days of September. Õppeaasta means “academic year”.
examples: Head õppeaasta algust! — Have a good start to the school year! • Soovin kõigile head õppeaasta algust! — I wish everyone a good start to the school year!
reply: Aitäh! — Thank you!

usage: A friendly slang greeting, mostly among young people. Used with friends and people your age — not with a shop assistant, a teacher or an adult you don’t know. Jou is also used to get someone’s attention: “hey, listen”.
examples: Jou, vennas! — Yo, bro! • Jou, kuule, kus vets on? — Hey, listen, where’s the toilet?
reply: Jou! — Yo! • Tšau! — Hi!

usage: An affectionate form of tšau — both “hi” and “bye”. Used with people close to you: friends and family. Not with a teacher or in a shop. Also written tšauki.
examples: Tsauki, kuidas läks? — Hiya, how did it go? • Olgu, tsauki siis! — OK, bye-bye then!
reply: Tsauki! — Hiya! / Bye!

usage: A common question to a friend right after a greeting — in person, on the phone or in a messenger. It is more of a friendly “how are you?”, so a short answer is enough.
examples: Jou, mis teed? — Yo, what are you up to? • Mis sa täna õhtul teed? — What are you doing this evening?
reply: Ei midagi erilist. Aga sina? — Nothing special. And you? • Õpin eesti keelt! — I’m learning Estonian!

usage: The shortest “good morning” — very casual: for family, friends or a flatmate. A bit more polite: Hommikust!, in full: Tere hommikust!
examples: Hommik! Kas kohvi on? — Morning! Is there any coffee? • Hommik, unimüts! — Morning, sleepyhead!
reply: Hommik! — Morning! • Hommikust! — Morning!

usage: A light, playful “hey” — both when meeting and when leaving. Similar to Finnish heippa. Variants include heipa and heipahei. Only for friends and in messages.
examples: Heips! Kaua pole näinud! — Hey! Long time no see! • Heips, homme näeme! — Bye, see you tomorrow!
reply: Heips! — Hey! • Tšau! — Hi!
